prompt: ok so i have a real problem. last year i decided i was going to learn spanish and i did duolingo for like 3 months and i watched a bunch of youtube videos and i felt like i was making progress but then i went on a trip to mexico and realized i literally couldnt understand or say anything useful. earlier this year i tried to pick up piano, bought a keyboard, watched some videos, tried to learn this one chopin piece because it sounded cool, and now the keyboard is sitting in the corner. like every time i start something i get really excited and watch a ton of videos and it feels like im learning but then a few weeks in i realize i cant actually do anything and i get discouraged and quit. whats wrong with how im approaching this and how do i actually learn a new skill without this happening again? im open to specific advice.

assertions.text: Diagnoses the user's passive-consumption / watch-videos-feels-like-learning pattern explicitly
Names the 'illusion of comprehension' / recognition-vs-recall distinction (following along is not knowing)
Explains why Duolingo / YouTube videos produce felt progress without transferable skill
Diagnoses attempting an advanced target (Chopin piece) without prerequisite/foundational skill
Includes a concrete daily session structure with time allocations
Prescribes high active-production to passive-intake ratio (e.g., 3:1 or stated numerically)
Includes spaced / distributed review of previously-learned material
Includes retrieval-based practice or self-testing without looking at notes
Names specific resources or tool types (e.g., Anki, tutor/language partner, a specific course)
Warns that the right approach will feel harder/slower than what they were doing before (desirable difficulty)
Explicitly recommends focusing on ONE skill rather than multiple simultaneously
Provides a concrete starting template or plan (not just principles) they can act on
